## Part II:
```{r}
communities <- read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_areas_of_Chicago")
```
Reads the page into r

```{r}
df_communities <- communities %>%
  html_element("table") %>%
  html_table%>%
  janitor::clean_names()
```
Calls the table from the datapage and uses the element function to scrape the table from the page into a neat table

```{r}
df_communities <- df_communities %>%
  slice(-(1), -(n()))

df_communities <- df_communities %>%
  rename(
    area_sqmi = area_9,
    area_km = area_9_2,
    density_sqmi = density,
    density_km = density_2
  )

df_communities$population <- gsub("[,]","", df_communities$population)
df_communities$population <-as.numeric(df_communities$population)
```
Cleans the dataframe by cleaning the column names, removing additional rows and removing the commas from population in order to change population data type to numeric 

```{r}
print(df_communities[df_communities$no == 24, ])
```
Prints the row for west town
```{r}
print(head(df_communities[order(df_communities$population, decreasing = TRUE), ], 5))
```
Prints the top 5 most populated areas in Chicago

```{r}
url <- read_html("https://books.toscrape.com/")
```
Reads the link in r
```{r}
books <- url %>%
  html_elements(".product_pod")
```
Sections where information is located
```{r}
titles <- books %>%
  html_elements("h3 a") %>%
  html_attr("title")
titles
```
Pulls the title names into a list
```{r}
price <- books%>%
  html_elements(".price_color")%>%
  html_text2()
price
```
Pulls the price of the books into a list
```{r}

availability <- books %>%
  html_elements(".availability.instock")%>%
  html_text2()
availability
```
Pulls the avaliability of the book into a list
```{r}
books_20 <- tibble(
  title = titles,
  price = price,
  availability = availability
)
books_20
```
pulls all the elements into a table
```{r}
rating <- books %>%
  html_elements(".star-rating")%>%
  html_attr("class")

rating <- gsub("star-rating", "", rating)
rating

```
Add in rating column as a bonus 

```{r}
rating_num <- c(" One" = 1, " Two" = 2, " Three" = 3, " Four" = 4, " Five" = 5)

rating <- as.numeric(rating_num[rating])
rating
```
Had to create a vector so the written numbers could know which numeric values they belonged to and assign them

```{r}
books_20_bonus <- tibble(
  title = titles,
  price = price,
  availability = availability, 
  rating = rating
)
books_20_bonus
```
Final bonus table

## Part III

```{r}
library(httr)
library(jsonlite)
```
Loads the needed libraries
```{r}
url <- "https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/v6vf-nfxy.json"

params <- list(
    community_area = "24",
    '$where' = "created_date >= '2026-01-01T00:00:00'",
    '$order' = "created_date DESC",
    '$limit' = 1000
    )

response <- GET(url, query = params)
```
Requests the data from the url and put parameters around certain variables, like filtering

```{r}
df <- fromJSON(content(response, "text", encoding = "UTF-8"))

print(nrow(df))
```
```{r}
print(colnames(df))
```
Creates the dataframe from the information and prints the number of rows of the dataframe as well as the column names

```{r}
sr_counts <- df %>%
  count(sr_type, sort =TRUE)%>%
  slice_head( n = 10)%>%
  print()
```
Creates a count of different service requests types, put them in descending order and found the top ten most common.  

A: This summary suggests that the neighborhood overwhelming needs graffiti removal more than any other service. The requests for graffiti removal is more than 3x that of the second most common request. This data cannot tell us which areas of West Town are the most common spots for these requests. 

## Part IV
The variables:    
Gross rent as a Percentage of Household Income, "Total": B25070_001E
Gross rent as a Percentage of Household Income, "50.0 percent or more": B25070_010E
Median Household Income: B19013_001E

```{r}
install.packages("tidycensus")
library(tidycensus)
library (tidyverse)
tidycensus::census_api_key("229ded5845ed56959b820d23b3361218ccb17e65", install = TRUE)
```
To load any necessary libraries

```{r}
readRenviron("~/.Renviron")

ohio_counties <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  state = "OH",
  year = 2024,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide",
  variables = c(
    gross_rent_total = "B25070_001",
    gross_rent_50pct = "B25070_010",
    median_household_income = "B19013_001"
  ),
)%>%
  select(
    GEOID, NAME, gross_rent_totalE, gross_rent_50pctE, median_household_incomeE
    )

ohio_counties
```
Retrieves the three variables for each county in Ohio. Kept variables with "E" for estimates and removed "M" variables which stood for margin of error but doesnt seem to be necessary for the dataframe.Made the dataframe wide to have all three variables side-by-side

```{r}
ohio_counties <- ohio_counties%>%
  mutate(
    severe_burden_rate = 
      (gross_rent_50pctE / gross_rent_totalE) * 100
    )
ohio_counties
```
Mutates the gross rent 50% variable divided gross rental total and multiples it by 100 to create a new variable called, "severe_burden_rate"

```{r}
ohio_counties <- ohio_counties%>%
  arrange(desc(severe_burden_rate))

ohio_counties
```
Arranges the counties severe burden rate from highest to lowest. Athens county is the highest.

```{r}
ohio_counties%>%
  summarise(
    mean_severe_burden_rate = mean(severe_burden_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_severe_burden_rate = median(severe_burden_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```
This code computes the mean and median of the severe burden rate in Ohio

```{r}
selected_counties <- bind_rows(
  ohio_counties %>% slice_max(severe_burden_rate, n=5, with_ties = FALSE),
  ohio_counties %>% slice_min(severe_burden_rate, n=5, with_ties = FALSE)
)%>%
  distinct(NAME, .keep_all = TRUE)

selected_counties
```
This code identifies the counties with the highest and lowest severe burden rates in Ohio

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(ohio_counties, aes(x=median_household_incomeE,
                          y=severe_burden_rate))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se= TRUE)+
  labs(
    title = "Severe Rent Burden vs Median Household Income in Ohio Counties",
    x = "Median Household Income (dollars)",
    y = "Households Paying 50% or more Income Toward Rent (%)"
  )+
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(selected_counties, aes(x = reorder(NAME, severe_burden_rate), 
                             y = severe_burden_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Highest and Lowest Severe Rent Burden Rates by Ohio County",
    x = "County",
    y = "Severe Burden Rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
This code creates a bar chart of the 10 most extreme values of the severe burden rate. I utilized the dataframe I created from the previous min and max step.
